intro: Two days before the cross, Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives and looked across the valley at the temple. Four of His disciples had just admired its great stones. He told them that not one stone would be left on another. Then they asked Him three questions: when will this happen, what will be the sign of your coming, and what will mark the end of the age? His answer fills Matthew 24 and 25. This study walks through that answer verse by verse, as fulfilled-prophecy (preterist) interpreters read it. The fulfilled reading makes one main claim. Jesus was speaking to these men about events they would live to see. He said that 'this generation' would not pass away before all these things happened (Matthew 24:34). About forty years later, in AD 70, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and burned the temple. This reading holds that the false messiahs, wars, persecution, flight, siege and judgment of the discourse all belong to those forty years. It also reads the language of the sun darkening and the Son of Man coming on the clouds as Old Testament judgment language, not as a picture of the end of the physical world. Why does this matter? If the reading is right, Jesus kept His word to the very people He spoke to. The discourse then becomes a record of His faithfulness, not a timetable of fear. Believers are freed to stop reading the news for signs, and to give themselves to the work of His kingdom. You do not have to agree with every step to learn from it. Read the text slowly, ask the five simple questions, weigh the ancient historians, and see each verse alongside how other Christians read it. Then decide for yourself.
orthodoxy: Where does this reading sit among Christians? It helps to separate two forms of it. Partial preterists hold that most of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in the Jewish War of AD 66-70. This includes the great tribulation and the judgment on the temple. But they still expect a future, bodily return of Christ, a general resurrection of the dead, and a final judgment. Writers such as Kenneth Gentry, R. C. Sproul and Keith Mathison hold this view. Many of them place the turn to the final coming at Matthew 24:36 or in Matthew 25:31-46. Full preterists (sometimes called 'covenant eschatology'; critics call it 'hyper-preterism') go further. They hold that the Second Coming, the resurrection and the judgment were also fulfilled in connection with AD 70. The reading presented in this study follows that fuller form, since it applies Matthew 25, including the judgment of the sheep and the goats, to the first century. This fuller form stands outside the historic creeds. The Apostles' Creed confesses that Christ 'will come to judge the living and the dead' and affirms 'the resurrection of the body'. The Nicene Creed says that He will come again in glory to judge, and that the church looks for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Critics give several reasons for rejecting full preterism. First, the whole church in every age has confessed a future return and resurrection. Second, Paul teaches a bodily resurrection in which death itself, the last enemy, is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:26, 15:54), and death is still with us. Third, the angels promised that Jesus would come back in the same way He went up (Acts 1:11). Fourth, Paul warned against Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Fifth, the Lord's Supper proclaims His death 'until He comes' (1 Corinthians 11:26), and the church has kept it ever since. Full preterists reply in turn. They say the creeds are valuable summaries but stand under Scripture, and that Scripture's time statements must decide the matter. They read the resurrection of 1 Corinthians 15 as the raising of God's people out of the realm of death at the close of the old covenant age, or as believers receiving new life at death. They note that 2 Timothy was written before AD 70, so Hymenaeus was wrong because he spoke too early, not because the resurrection was never near. They read Acts 1:11 as a promise that He would come in clouds, as He left in a cloud. And they hold that 'until He comes' fitted a church that lived before AD 70. Partial preterists agree with full preterists on much of Matthew 24 but side with the creeds on these points. Futurist, historicist and idealist readers see the discourse differently again. To compare all these views side by side, see the app's Olivet Discourse study.

keys.question: Who is speaking, and to whom?
keys.answer: Jesus is speaking. Matthew 24:3 says only that 'the disciples' came to Him privately. Mark 13:3 names them: Peter, James, John and Andrew, two pairs of brothers. The fulfilled reading stresses that the word 'you' in the discourse first means these four men. Matthew, a former tax collector and one of the Twelve, later wrote it down for early believers, many of them Jewish.

keys.question: What is the discourse about?
keys.answer: It begins with the temple. Jesus says it will be thrown down. The disciples then ask when this will be, what the sign of His coming will be, and what the end of the age will be. The answer covers deceivers, wars, persecution, the 'abomination of desolation', a great tribulation, the coming of the Son of Man, the fig tree lesson, and parables about readiness. The fulfilled reading takes 'the end of the age' as the end of the old covenant age centred on the temple, not the end of the world.

keys.question: Where is Jesus, and where will these things happen?
keys.answer: He is sitting on the Mount of Olives, a ridge east of Jerusalem that looks across the Kidron Valley to the temple. The places named in the discourse are local: the holy place, Judea, its mountains, flat housetops and fields. Luke adds Jerusalem surrounded by armies. The fulfilled reading sees this local detail as a clue that the warnings concern Judea and Jerusalem in that century.

keys.question: When did Jesus speak, and when would it happen?
keys.answer: He spoke in the last week before the cross, in the spring of about AD 30 or AD 33, depending on the chronology used. He set the time limit Himself: 'this generation' would not pass away until all these things took place. The Jewish revolt began in AD 66. Titus besieged Jerusalem in the spring and summer of AD 70, and the temple burned in late summer of that year, about forty years later.

keys.question: Why did Jesus give this teaching?
keys.answer: To prepare His followers. He warned them not to be deceived by false messiahs, told them to endure, and gave them a clear signal to flee to the mountains. The fall of Jerusalem was one of the worst disasters in Jewish history, and the city and temple were the centre of Jewish life. Jesus wanted His people ready, faithful and alive. The parables of Matthew 25 add that they should be watchful, faithful with what He gave them, and kind to the least of His brothers.

historians.name: Flavius Josephus
historians.life: Born in Jerusalem about AD 37 into a priestly family; died about AD 100, probably in Rome.
historians.works: The Jewish War (written in the 70s AD), Antiquities of the Jews (about AD 93-94), his Life, and Against Apion.
historians.role: Josephus is the main eyewitness of the war. He commanded Jewish forces in Galilee, surrendered to Vespasian at Jotapata in AD 67, and later served Titus as an interpreter during the siege of Jerusalem. His Jewish War describes the false prophets, the factions, the famine, the burning of the temple (Jewish War 6.4.5-8) and the numbers of the dead and captured (Jewish War 6.9.3). The fulfilled reading relies on him more than on any other ancient writer. His Antiquities also mentions John the Baptist (18.5.2), James the brother of Jesus (20.9.1) and, in a disputed passage, Jesus Himself (18.3.3).
historians.caution: Josephus wrote under Roman patronage and wanted to flatter Vespasian and Titus. He blames the war on a few Jewish rebels and paints himself in a good light. Ancient writers often rounded or inflated large numbers, so his figures (such as 1,100,000 dead) are debated. He never mentions the Olivet Discourse, so links between his account and Jesus' words are drawn by interpreters.

historians.name: Cornelius Tacitus
historians.life: About AD 56 to about AD 120. A Roman senator who became consul in AD 97 and later governed the province of Asia.
historians.works: The Histories (covering AD 69-96, much of it lost) and the Annals (covering AD 14-68, partly lost), plus shorter works such as Agricola and Germania.
historians.role: Tacitus is an independent Roman witness. In Histories 5.1-13 he describes the Jews, the start of Titus' siege, and strange signs reported in the temple. In Histories 5.13 he says many Jews believed ancient priestly writings foretold that men from Judea would rule the world at that time. In Annals 15.44 he tells of Nero blaming the Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64 and mentions 'Christus', executed under Pontius Pilate. He also records the earthquake that struck Laodicea in AD 60 (Annals 14.27).
historians.caution: Tacitus was not an eyewitness of the war, and he wrote about thirty years later. He openly despised Jews and Christians. His account of the siege breaks off near its start, so his description of the fall itself is lost.

historians.name: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus
historians.life: About AD 69 to after AD 122. A scholar and imperial secretary under Trajan and Hadrian.
historians.works: The Lives of the Caesars (often called The Twelve Caesars), about AD 121: biographies from Julius Caesar to Domitian.
historians.role: Suetonius supplies the background of the emperors who ruled during the New Testament period. In Vespasian 4.5 he says that an old and settled belief spread through the East that men from Judea would rule the world at that time, and that the Jews applied it to themselves and revolted. He also mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome (Claudius 25.4, compare Acts 18:2) and Nero punishing Christians (Nero 16.2).
historians.caution: Suetonius was not an eyewitness. He loved anecdotes and gossip, and he organised his lives by topic rather than by date. He gives few details of the Jewish War itself.

historians.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
historians.life: About AD 260 to about AD 339. Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine.
historians.works: The Church History (completed about AD 324-325), the Chronicle, and the Life of Constantine.
historians.role: Eusebius is the first great historian of the church. He preserves the report that Jerusalem's Christians were warned to leave the city before the war and settled in Pella, east of the Jordan (Church History 3.5.3). He quotes Josephus at length on the siege and famine (3.5-3.8) and presents the fall of Jerusalem as judgment for the rejection of Christ. He also records Irenaeus' statement that John saw the Revelation near the end of Domitian's reign (3.18; 5.8), which is central to the debate on Revelation's date.
historians.caution: Eusebius wrote more than 250 years after the events. He often depended on earlier writers whose works are now lost, and he wrote with a clear theological purpose. Some scholars question the Pella tradition, though others defend its historical core.

context.title: The King arrives
context.text: Holy Week begins with Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt. Matthew says this fulfils Zechariah 9:9, the humble king coming to Zion. The crowds hail Him as the Son of David. The fulfilled reading notes that the King has come to His city. What follows is His final appeal to it, and then His verdict on it.

context.title: The temple cleansed
context.text: Jesus drives out those who buy and sell in the temple courts. He joins Isaiah 56:7 (a house of prayer) with Jeremiah 7:11 (a den of robbers). In Jeremiah 7 that charge came just before the first temple was destroyed. Many interpreters see a warning here: the second temple was heading for the same end.

context.title: The fruitless fig tree
context.text: Jesus finds leaves but no fruit on a fig tree, and it withers. Many interpreters read this as an acted parable. In the prophets the fig tree can picture Israel (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10). A nation full of religious show but without fruit faces judgment. Jesus adds that faith could say to 'this mountain' be thrown into the sea, which some take as a hint at the temple mount. Others read the sign more generally, as a lesson about empty religion that hides sin instead of removing it.

context.title: The tenants and the son
context.text: A landowner sends servants to collect fruit from his vineyard. The tenants beat and kill them, and at last kill his son. In the story, God is the owner, the leaders of Israel are the tenants, the prophets are the servants, and Jesus is the son. Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone that becomes the cornerstone. He then says the kingdom will be taken from them and given to a people who produce its fruit (Matthew 21:43). The leaders understood that He was speaking about them.

context.title: The wedding feast and the burned city
context.text: A king prepares a wedding feast for his son. Those invited refuse, and some kill his servants. The king sends his armies, destroys those murderers and burns their city (Matthew 22:7). Then the invitation goes out to everyone in the streets. The fulfilled reading sees the burned city as Jerusalem in AD 70, and the new guests as the Gentiles who came into the church.

context.title: Questions in the temple
context.text: Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees and a lawyer each try to trap Jesus: on taxes to Caesar, on the resurrection, and on the greatest commandment. He answers each one, then asks how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord (Psalm 110:1). After that, no one dares to question Him. The leaders have rejected Him, and the stage is set for His judgment speech.

context.title: The woes and 'this generation'
context.text: Jesus pronounces a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees, in the style of the prophets (Isaiah 5:8-23; Habakkuk 2:6-19). Some manuscripts count eight woes, most modern texts seven. He tells them to fill up the measure of their fathers, who killed the prophets. All the righteous blood shed on the earth, from Abel to Zechariah, will come on them. Then He says that all these things will come upon this generation (Matthew 23:36). The fulfilled reading treats this as the key to chapter 24. The same people, and the same time limit, are in view.

context.title: Your house is left desolate
context.text: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets. He longed to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks, but they would not come. Then He says, 'Your house is left to you desolate.' The 'house' is most likely the temple. In the very next verse, Jesus leaves the temple and the disciples point out its buildings (Matthew 24:1). The chapter break hides how closely these scenes belong together.

chapters.title: The setting: the King and His city
chapters.summary: Before Matthew 24, read Matthew 21-23. Jesus enters Jerusalem as king, cleanses the temple, curses a fruitless fig tree, and tells parables of rejected servants and a burned city. He ends with woes on the leaders, the promise that all these things will come on 'this generation', and the words 'your house is left to you desolate'. The discourse grows out of this setting.

chapters.title: Not one stone on another
chapters.summary: Jesus leaves the temple. The disciples point out its great buildings. He says every stone will be thrown down. In AD 70 Titus' army burned the temple and later levelled the city. The Arch of Titus in Rome still shows the temple lampstand carried in triumph.

chapters.title: The beginning of birth pains
chapters.summary: The disciples ask when, what sign, and what end. Jesus warns of false messiahs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, betrayal and false prophets. But the end is not yet. First the gospel must be preached in the whole inhabited world. The fulfilled reading finds each of these in Acts, the letters and Josephus between AD 30 and 70.

chapters.title: The abomination and the great tribulation
chapters.summary: When they see the abomination of desolation, those in Judea must flee at once. Jesus describes a distress worse than any before or after, days cut short for the elect, and false christs with signs. The fulfilled reading links this to Jerusalem surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20), the flight to Pella, and the siege of AD 70.

chapters.title: The Son of Man coming on the clouds
chapters.summary: Sun and moon darken, stars fall, and the tribes mourn as they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds. The fulfilled reading hears the language of the prophets, who used such pictures for the fall of nations, and reads it as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem and the gathering of His people through the gospel.

chapters.title: This generation will not pass away
chapters.summary: Learn from the fig tree: when you see these things, He is near, at the doors. This generation will not pass away until all these things happen. Heaven and earth will pass away, but His words will not. The fulfilled reading holds that this verse sets the time for everything before it.

chapters.title: No one knows the day or the hour
chapters.summary: The exact day and hour are known only to the Father. As in Noah's day, people will carry on with life until judgment sweeps them away. One will be taken and one left. So keep watch, like a householder expecting a thief. The fulfilled reading sees the generation as fixed but the day unknown, and the one 'taken' as taken in judgment.

chapters.title: The faithful and the wicked servant
chapters.summary: A faithful servant feeds the household until his master comes. A wicked servant says 'my master is delayed', beats his fellow servants and lives with drunkards. The master comes unexpectedly and punishes him with the hypocrites. The fulfilled reading sees a warning to leaders in that generation.

chapters.title: Three parables of the end of the age
chapters.summary: Ten virgins wait for the bridegroom. Servants are given talents to trade with until their master returns. The Son of Man sits on His throne and divides the sheep from the goats by how they treated the least of His brothers. The fulfilled reading, in its full form, applies all three to the coming of Christ in that generation.

verses.title: The disciples admire the Temple
verses.phrase: shew him the buildings of the temple
verses.meaning: Jesus has just pronounced woes on the leaders and said their house is left desolate (Matthew 23:38). Now He walks out of the Temple. The disciples point to its great buildings, as if to ask how such a place could ever fall. In the fulfilled reading, His leaving the Temple is a sign that God's presence is departing from it.
verses.fulfilment: Herod the Great began rebuilding the Temple in about 20/19 BC. Work on the wider complex went on for decades and was only finished in about AD 63-64, under the governor Albinus. So the great buildings were completed only a few years before the Romans destroyed them in AD 70.

evidence.text: Josephus says Herod began the rebuilding in the eighteenth year of his reign.
Josephus reports that the work was finished under Albinus, and about 18,000 workers lost their jobs.
Josephus describes huge white stones and a front covered with gold that shone like the sun.

verses.other: Most readers of every view agree that this verse describes Herod's Temple. Futurist readers usually see the setting as the start of a discourse that later moves to a distant end-time.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader agrees on the setting and adds that nothing in the scene suggests a change of subject. The disciples ask about the building in front of them.

verses.title: Not one stone upon another
verses.phrase: There shall not be left here one stone upon another
verses.meaning: Jesus answers the disciples' admiration with a plain prediction. The whole Temple complex they are looking at will be torn down. The word 'here' points to the buildings in front of them. The fulfilled reading takes this as the anchor of the whole discourse: everything that follows answers when and how this would happen.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 70 the Roman army under Titus captured Jerusalem. The Temple burned on the ninth or tenth of the month Av, about late August AD 70. Titus then ordered the city and Temple to be razed. The Arch of Titus in Rome, built after his death in AD 81, shows soldiers carrying away the Temple's lampstand.

evidence.text: Josephus says the Temple burned on the tenth of the month Lous (Av), the same day the first Temple had burned.
Josephus says Titus ordered the city and Temple demolished. Only three towers and part of the western city wall were left standing.
The relief on the arch shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah and other Temple objects in triumph.

verses.other: Futurist readers agree that this verse was fulfilled in AD 70. Some point to the large stones still standing in the Western Wall and say the prophecy was not completed in every detail.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the Western Wall is part of the retaining wall of the Temple platform, not the Temple buildings the disciples showed Jesus. Those buildings were completely destroyed.

verses.title: One question about the Temple
verses.phrase: what shall be the sign of thy coming
verses.meaning: On the Mount of Olives, four disciples ask privately: when will these things happen, and what will be the sign of His coming and of the end of the age? The fulfilled reading treats this as one question with three parts, all tied to the Temple's fall. 'The end of the age' means the end of the Old Covenant age with its Temple and sacrifices, not the end of the planet.
verses.fulfilment: The discourse was spoken in the last week of Jesus' ministry, about AD 30 or 33. Within about forty years the Temple was destroyed in AD 70. With it, the sacrifices of the Mosaic system came to an end.

evidence.text: Josephus records that the daily sacrifice in the Temple stopped during the siege of AD 70 for lack of men to offer it.

word.note: The disciples ask about the 'end of the age' (synteleia tou aionos), not the end of the world (kosmos). The fulfilled reading sees the age as the Old Covenant era. Hebrews 9:26 says Christ appeared 'at the end of the ages', in the first century.

verses.other: Futurist readers often see the question as two or three separate questions. They hold that Jesus answers the Temple question in part and then speaks about a coming at the end of world history.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that Mark and Luke record only a question about 'these things'. This suggests the disciples expected the coming and the end of the age to happen with the Temple's fall.

verses.title: Do not be deceived
verses.phrase: Take heed that no man deceive you
verses.meaning: Jesus' first word is a warning about deception. In the fulfilled reading, 'you' means the disciples sitting with Him. Mark 13:3 names them: Peter, James, John and Andrew. The warning prepared them for a real danger in their own lifetime. The apostles later passed the same warning on to the early churches.
verses.fulfilment: In the years before AD 70, many teachers and leaders drew people away with false hopes. Paul warned the churches not to be shaken by false reports (2 Thessalonians 2:2-3). Some interpreters in this reading identify Paul's 'man of lawlessness' with a figure of the Jewish War, such as Titus or the Zealot leaders. Others in the same reading disagree.

evidence.text: Josephus describes deceivers who claimed divine inspiration and led crowds astray under the governor Felix.

verses.other: Futurist readers see the 'you' as the disciples standing for all believers, especially those alive at the end of history.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader agrees the lesson applies to every Christian. But the first meaning belongs to the people Jesus addressed, who would see these things.

verses.title: Many will claim to be the Christ
verses.phrase: many shall come in my name, saying, I am Christ
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that many will come using His name or claiming the role of Messiah. The fulfilled reading points to the many impostors and would-be deliverers who appeared in Judea between Jesus' death and AD 70. The New Testament itself names some of them.
verses.fulfilment: About AD 44-46 Theudas led a crowd to the Jordan, promising the river would part. Under Felix, in the mid-50s, an Egyptian prophet gathered followers on the Mount of Olives. He promised that Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command. Roman troops killed or scattered both groups.

evidence.text: Josephus says Theudas claimed to be a prophet and promised to divide the Jordan. The governor Fadus sent cavalry, and Theudas was beheaded.
Josephus says an Egyptian false prophet led a crowd to the Mount of Olives. Felix attacked and most were killed or captured.
A Roman officer asks Paul if he is the Egyptian who led 4,000 'assassins' into the wilderness.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect a great increase of false messiahs before Christ's return, and many see a final Antichrist in view.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader points out that John already said 'many antichrists have come' and that it was 'the last hour' (1 John 2:18). The warning was being fulfilled in the apostles' own day.

verses.title: Wars and rumours of wars
verses.phrase: ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars
verses.meaning: Jesus tells the disciples not to panic when they hear of wars, because 'the end is not yet'. In the fulfilled reading, 'the end' is the end of the age asked about in verse 3: the fall of the Temple. Wars and threats of war would come first, but they were not the final sign.
verses.fulfilment: Jesus spoke during the Roman peace (Pax Romana). In AD 40 Caligula ordered his statue placed in the Temple, and war nearly broke out. In AD 66 the Jewish revolt began. In AD 68-69, after Nero's death, Rome itself fell into civil war, with four emperors in one year.

evidence.text: Josephus describes Caligula's order to set up his statue in the Temple and the alarm it caused in Judea.
Tacitus describes the period as full of disasters, savage battles and civil strife, with four emperors killed.

verses.other: Futurist readers see an increase of wars across the world as a general sign of the age, growing stronger before Christ returns.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus spoke to people who would 'hear' of these wars. Within forty years the peaceful empire was shaken by revolt and civil war, just as He said.

verses.title: Famines, pestilences and earthquakes
verses.phrase: famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places
verses.meaning: Jesus foretells conflict between nations and kingdoms, along with famines, diseases and earthquakes in various places. The fulfilled reading looks for these within the Roman world before AD 70. It finds them recorded both in Acts and in Roman and Jewish historians.
verses.fulfilment: A severe famine struck Judea under Claudius, about AD 46-48, as Agabus had predicted (Acts 11:28). Earthquakes shook the Roman province of Asia and Italy: Laodicea in AD 60 and Pompeii in Campania in AD 62. A plague in Rome in AD 65 killed many thousands. In AD 66, Jews and Syrians fought in many cities.

evidence.text: Josephus says Queen Helena of Adiabene bought grain from Egypt for Jerusalem during a great famine.
Tacitus records that Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in AD 60 and rebuilt from its own resources.
Tacitus describes a deadly plague in Rome in AD 65.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect these troubles to grow in number and strength in the last days before Christ's return.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that such events have happened in every age. Jesus gave them to His hearers as signs they would see within their own lifetime.

verses.title: The beginning of birth pains
verses.phrase: All these are the beginning of sorrows
verses.meaning: Jesus calls these troubles the beginning of birth pains. Birth pains are painful, but they lead to new life. In the fulfilled reading, the old covenant order was passing away while the new covenant community was being born. The years from the cross to AD 70 were a time of transition.
verses.fulfilment: The forty years from about AD 30 to AD 70 saw the church grow while Jerusalem moved toward war. The pains grew stronger until the Temple fell. After that, the church stood clearly apart from the old Temple system.

word.note: The word describes the pains of a woman in labour. The prophets used it for a time of distress that ends in a new beginning (Isaiah 66:7-8). It suggests sharp pains that come closer together, followed by a birth.

verses.other: Futurist readers often link the birth pains to a final period of trouble before the Messiah's kingdom. Some connect them to a future seven-year tribulation.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the birth was near at hand. The new covenant people were coming to birth in the first century, and the old covenant was 'ready to vanish away' (Hebrews 8:13).

verses.title: Persecution and martyrdom
verses.phrase: ye shall be hated of all nations
verses.meaning: Jesus warns the disciples that they will be handed over, afflicted and killed, and hated by all nations for His name. The fulfilled reading sees this fulfilled in the persecutions recorded in Acts and in Roman history. These came first from Jerusalem's leaders and later from Rome.
verses.fulfilment: Stephen was stoned in Jerusalem, perhaps about AD 34. James son of Zebedee was killed by Herod Agrippa I in about AD 44. James the brother of Jesus was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62. In AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians for the great fire of Rome.

evidence.text: Josephus says the high priest Ananus had James, 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ', and others stoned.
Tacitus says the Christians were hated for their supposed crimes and were punished by Nero.
Eusebius records the death of James the Just in Jerusalem.

verses.other: Futurist readers often see a final, worldwide persecution of believers in the end times, in addition to past persecutions.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that Jesus spoke to 'you', the disciples. Most of the apostles did suffer and die for His name, just as He said.

verses.title: Betrayal and hatred
verses.phrase: shall betray one another, and shall hate one another
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that many will fall away and betray and hate one another. In the fulfilled reading, the pressure of persecution would cause some believers to turn against others. Some would give their names to the authorities to save themselves.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 64 Nero arrested Christians after the fire of Rome. Tacitus says those first arrested gave information, and a 'huge crowd' was then convicted. Many were cruelly killed. Christian tradition, recorded later by Eusebius, says Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero.

evidence.text: Tacitus says that on the information of those first seized, a huge crowd was convicted. Some were burned as torches at night.
Eusebius records the tradition that Paul was beheaded and Peter crucified in Rome under Nero.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect a great falling away from the faith at the end of the age, often linked to 2 Thessalonians 2:3.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader answers that Paul already wrote that all in Asia had turned away from him (2 Timothy 1:15). The falling away Jesus described happened in the apostles' generation.

verses.title: False prophets deceive many
verses.phrase: many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that many false prophets will arise and lead many astray. In the fulfilled reading, these are the false prophets who promised deliverance to Jerusalem during the war. Their false hopes kept people in the city until it was too late.
verses.fulfilment: During the siege of AD 70, the rebel leaders hired prophets to tell the people to wait for help from God. This stopped people from deserting to the Romans. On the day the Temple burned, a false prophet led a crowd up to the Temple to receive 'signs of deliverance'. They died there.

evidence.text: Josephus says the rebel leaders bribed many false prophets to tell the people to wait for God's help, so they would not desert.
Josephus describes deceivers who led crowds into the wilderness, promising signs of freedom.

verses.other: Futurist readers see false prophets increasing in the last days, often linked to the false prophet of Revelation 13.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that John said 'many false prophets have gone out into the world' already (1 John 4:1). Josephus shows how these deceivers led many to their deaths.

verses.title: Love grows cold
verses.phrase: the love of many shall wax cold
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that because lawlessness will increase, the love of many will grow cold. The fulfilled reading sees this in the spiritual condition of first-century Judea and of some churches. Jesus had already called His hearers 'a wicked and adulterous generation' (Matthew 12:39).
verses.fulfilment: During the war, rival rebel groups in Jerusalem fought and killed one another. From AD 68 the Zealots murdered leading citizens, including the former high priest Ananus. Josephus says no city ever suffered such things and no generation was ever more wicked.

evidence.text: Josephus says no other city ever suffered such misery, and no generation since the world began was more fruitful in wickedness.
Josephus records the murder of the former high priest Ananus by the Zealots and their Idumean allies.

verses.other: Futurist readers see growing lawlessness and loss of love as marks of the last days before Christ's return.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that Paul's 'last days' warning was given to Timothy, who was told to turn away from such people (2 Timothy 3:5). The warning fit their own time.

verses.title: Endure to the end
verses.phrase: he that shall endure unto the end
verses.meaning: Jesus promises that the one who endures to the end will be saved. In the fulfilled reading, 'the end' is the end of the age in AD 70. 'Saved' here mainly means being rescued from the coming destruction. Believers who held on to His words and fled at the right time would escape alive.
verses.fulfilment: Eusebius records that the Jerusalem church received a warning before the war and left the city. They settled in Pella, a town east of the Jordan. So the Christians of Jerusalem escaped the siege and the slaughter of AD 70.

evidence.text: Eusebius says the Jerusalem church was told by a revelation to leave the city before the war and to live in Pella of Perea.

word.note: The word often means rescue from physical danger, as in Matthew 8:25 ('Lord, save us'). Here the verb for 'endure' is hypomeno, to remain or hold firm. Together they promise rescue for those who stay faithful.

verses.other: Futurist readers usually take 'the end' as the end of a believer's life or the end of history. They see 'saved' as final salvation.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the context is the end of the age asked about in verse 3. Luke 21:18-19 speaks of physical survival: 'not a hair of your head will perish'.

verses.title: The gospel to the whole world
verses.phrase: preached in all the world for a witness
verses.meaning: Jesus says the gospel of the kingdom will be preached in the whole world as a witness to all nations, and then the end will come. In the fulfilled reading, 'world' means the inhabited Roman world. The gospel had to reach it before the end of the Old Covenant age in AD 70.
verses.fulfilment: By the early 60s AD, Paul could say the gospel was bearing fruit 'in all the world' (Colossians 1:6). He said it had been preached 'to every creature under heaven' (Colossians 1:23). Churches existed in Judea, Syria, Asia Minor, Greece, Rome and Egypt. The Temple fell a few years later, in AD 70.

evidence.text: Paul says the gospel has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven.
Paul says the faith of the Roman believers is spoken of throughout the whole world.

word.note: This word is used in Luke 2:1, where Augustus orders 'all the world' to be registered. That meant the Roman Empire. It is also used in Acts 11:28 for a famine 'over all the world' under Claudius. The fulfilled reading takes it the same way here.

verses.other: Futurist readers see this as the task of world mission, still to be completed among every people group before Christ returns.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader agrees that mission continues today. But this verse uses Paul's own word for the known world. Paul said the task had already been done in his day.

verses.title: The abomination of desolation
verses.phrase: the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel
verses.meaning: Jesus gives the disciples a clear sign: when they see the 'abomination of desolation' that Daniel spoke of standing in the holy place, they must act. Luke's parallel explains it: 'when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies' (Luke 21:20). Fulfilled interpreters differ on details. Some point to the Roman armies, some to Zealot desecration of the Temple, and some to both.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 66 the Roman general Cestius Gallus surrounded Jerusalem and then withdrew. In AD 67-68 the Zealots occupied the Temple and appointed a high priest by lot. In AD 70, after the Temple burned, Roman soldiers set up their standards in the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them.

evidence.text: Josephus describes Cestius Gallus attacking Jerusalem in AD 66 and then suddenly withdrawing.
Josephus says the Zealots took over the Temple and chose an unfit man as high priest by lot.
Josephus says the Romans brought their standards into the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them.

word.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word often describes idols and idolatry. The phrase 'abomination of desolation' means a detestable thing that brings ruin. It comes from Daniel 9:27, 11:31 and 12:11.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect a future Antichrist to set up an idol or image in a rebuilt Temple, in the middle of a seven-year tribulation.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus said 'when you see', speaking to His disciples. Luke 21:20 explains the sign in terms of armies around Jerusalem, which they did see.

verses.title: Flee to the mountains
verses.phrase: let them which be in Judaea flee into the mountains
verses.meaning: Jesus tells those in Judea to flee to the mountains when they see the sign. In the fulfilled reading, this local detail shows the passage is about first-century Judea, not the whole world. The safe place was outside the doomed city.
verses.fulfilment: After Cestius Gallus withdrew from Jerusalem in late AD 66, many people left the city. Eusebius says the Christians went to Pella, east of the Jordan. When the siege came in AD 70, the believers were already gone.

evidence.text: Eusebius says the believers left Jerusalem before the war and lived in Pella, a city of Perea.
Josephus says that after Cestius' defeat many leading Jews left the city 'as from a sinking ship'.

verses.other: Futurist readers apply this to Jewish people in Israel at a future time. Some see the flight as a refuge in places like Petra.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the history matches closely. The sign came, there was a short break, and the believers fled before the city was shut in.

verses.title: Do not go back into the house
verses.phrase: Let him which is on the housetop not come down
verses.meaning: Jesus says the person on the roof must not go down to fetch belongings. Houses in Judea had flat roofs used for work, rest and prayer. The fulfilled reading sees this as practical advice for first-century people: when the sign comes, leave at once.
verses.fulfilment: In a Judean town, a person on a flat roof could see an approaching army. Outside stairs often led from the roof to the street. So a person could flee without going through the house. The danger grew quickly once Roman forces moved through Judea from AD 67 onward.
verses.other: Futurist readers take this as a picture of the speed needed in a future crisis. Some apply it to Israel at the end of the age.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that the details fit first-century Judea: flat roofs, outside stairs and towns near an advancing army.

verses.title: Do not go back for your cloak
verses.phrase: Neither let him which is in the field return back
verses.meaning: Jesus says the worker in the field must not return home for a cloak. A worker usually left the outer cloak at home or at the edge of the field. The fulfilled reading sees an urgent call to flee without delay, as Lot's family was told not to look back.
verses.fulfilment: Fields lay on open, lower ground, where workers would be easy to see. During Vespasian's campaigns of AD 67-68, Roman troops moved through the countryside of Galilee, Perea and Judea. Many people who delayed were killed or captured.

evidence.text: Josephus describes Roman forces in Perea in AD 68 killing and capturing many people who had fled from Gadara.

verses.other: Futurist readers see this as a warning for a future time of sudden danger, especially for Israel.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the setting is a farming land under threat of invasion. It matches Judea in the years AD 66-70.

verses.title: Woe to mothers
verses.phrase: woe unto them that are with child
verses.meaning: Jesus grieves for pregnant women and nursing mothers, who would find it hard to flee. The fulfilled reading links this with His words to the 'daughters of Jerusalem' on the way to the cross (Luke 23:28-29). Those days would bring great suffering to families.
verses.fulfilment: During the siege of AD 70 the famine in Jerusalem became terrible. Josephus tells of a woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, who killed and ate her own child. This recalls the curses of Deuteronomy 28:53-57.

evidence.text: Josephus tells of a woman in the siege who, starving and in despair, killed and ate her infant son.
Josephus describes how the famine destroyed whole families and how children snatched food from parents.

verses.other: Futurist readers apply this to mothers during a future great tribulation.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the warning was fulfilled in the siege of Jerusalem. Applying it to mothers today can cause needless fear.

verses.title: Not in winter or on the Sabbath
verses.phrase: pray ye that your flight be not in the winter
verses.meaning: Jesus tells the disciples to pray that their flight will not be in winter or on a Sabbath. Winter rain made roads hard and rivers high. On the Sabbath, city gates might be closed and travel was limited by custom. These details fit a Jewish setting in first-century Judea.
verses.fulfilment: In early AD 68, people fleeing from Gadara were trapped by the Jordan River, which was swollen by rain. Many drowned or were killed. Under the law, travel on the Sabbath was limited. Nehemiah had once shut Jerusalem's gates on the Sabbath.

evidence.text: Josephus says the Jordan was swollen with rain and the fleeing crowd could not cross. Many were killed or drowned.

word.note: The word means running away from danger. Jesus speaks of a real escape on foot from a real place. The concern about the Sabbath points to people living under Jewish custom in Judea.

verses.other: Futurist readers say the Sabbath detail shows that Jewish believers in a future Israel are in view.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the Sabbath detail fits the first-century disciples, who lived among Sabbath-keeping people in Judea. It does not need a distant future setting.

verses.title: Great tribulation
verses.phrase: then shall be great tribulation
verses.meaning: Jesus says there will be great distress, such as has not been since the beginning of the world, nor ever will be. The fulfilled reading sees this as the siege and fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. It was a unique judgment on the city and its Temple at the end of the Old Covenant age. Luke calls it 'wrath on this people' (Luke 21:23).
verses.fulfilment: Titus besieged Jerusalem from about April to September AD 70. Famine, civil war inside the city and Roman attacks killed vast numbers. The Temple burned in late August. Josephus gives 1,100,000 dead and 97,000 taken captive in the whole war.

evidence.text: Josephus says 97,000 were taken captive during the whole war and 1,100,000 died during the siege.
In his preface Josephus says the misfortunes of all people since the world began fall short of those of the Jews.

word.note: Here Jesus says 'since the beginning of the world (kosmos)'. This is a different word from oikoumene in verse 14. The phrase 'such as has not been … nor ever will be' is a familiar prophetic way to stress how severe a judgment is (compare Ezekiel 5:9).

verses.other: Futurist readers place the great tribulation in the future, as a worldwide time of trouble. Some also point out that later events, such as the Holocaust, killed more people.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that Jesus' words describe a covenant judgment on Jerusalem, not a contest of numbers. 'Nor ever will be' shows it was a one-time event.

verses.title: The days shortened
verses.phrase: except those days should be shortened
verses.meaning: Jesus says that if those days were not shortened, no one would survive. But for the sake of the elect, they will be cut short. In the fulfilled reading, 'no flesh' means no one in the land. 'The elect' are the believers, whom God protected.
verses.fulfilment: The war lasted from AD 66 to 70, about three and a half years. Cestius' sudden withdrawal in AD 66 gave believers time to flee. Titus' siege itself lasted only about five months. His quick wall around the city ended the siege faster than many expected.

evidence.text: Eusebius says the Jerusalem church escaped to Pella before the war.
Josephus says the Romans built a wall around the whole city in three days.
Josephus says Titus admitted that God had helped him take the city.

verses.other: Futurist readers see this as God limiting a future seven-year tribulation, so that some will survive until Christ returns.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader notes that the war on Judea lasted about three and a half years. Some in this reading link this to the 'forty-two months' of Revelation 13:5.

verses.title: Do not believe 'Here is the Christ'
verses.phrase: Lo, here is Christ, or there; believe it not
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that during the crisis people will say, 'Look, here is the Christ!' The disciples must not believe them. The fulfilled reading sees this as a warning aimed at the time of the war and siege. At that time leaders rose up claiming to bring deliverance.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 66 Menahem, a descendant of Judas the Galilean, entered the Temple dressed as a king, and was then killed. Later, Simon bar Giora led rebels in the city. When captured in AD 70, he appeared in white and purple robes. He was executed in Rome during Titus' triumph.

evidence.text: Josephus says Menahem went up to the Temple in royal clothing with armed followers, and was later killed.
Josephus says Simon bar Giora rose out of the ground at the Temple site dressed in white and purple.

verses.other: Futurist readers see this as a warning against claims of Christ's return in the last days before His real coming.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the setting is the time of the tribulation in Judea. In that time, men did claim royal and saving roles.

verses.title: Great signs and wonders
verses.phrase: shall shew great signs and wonders
verses.meaning: Jesus warns that false christs and false prophets will perform great signs to deceive, if possible, even the elect. The fulfilled reading points to the magicians and false prophets of Acts and to the prophets of the siege. They promised miracles of deliverance.
verses.fulfilment: Acts records Simon the sorcerer in Samaria and Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, in Cyprus. During the siege of AD 70, prophets told the people to wait for signs from God. On the day the Temple burned, a crowd followed one such promise to their deaths.

evidence.text: Josephus says many prophets were bribed to tell the people to wait for God's help. He says deceivers easily persuade people in distress.
Simon of Samaria amazed people with magic and claimed to be someone great.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect a future false prophet who will do great signs, as in Revelation 13:13-14.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the disciples needed this warning in their own day. The deceivers Josephus describes fit Jesus' words.

verses.title: Told beforehand
verses.phrase: Behold, I have told you before
verses.meaning: Jesus reminds the disciples that He has told them these things in advance. In the fulfilled reading, He speaks to men who would live through the events. He prepared them so they would not be caught by fear or deception. God reveals His plans to His servants before He acts.
verses.fulfilment: The Jerusalem believers remembered His warning about forty years later. They fled before the siege, as Eusebius records. The prophecy given in about AD 30-33 guided their actions in the crisis of AD 66-70.

evidence.text: Eusebius says the church left Jerusalem because of a revelation given before the war.

verses.other: Futurist readers see this as a word for believers in every age, especially those living at the end of history.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader agrees that all believers can learn from it. But 'I have told you' was spoken to the four disciples, who would see the events.

verses.title: Not in the desert or the inner rooms
verses.phrase: Behold, he is in the desert; go not forth
verses.meaning: Jesus warns: if people say the Messiah is in the wilderness, do not go out. If they say He is in the inner rooms, do not believe it. The fulfilled reading sees two kinds of false hope: leaders who led crowds into the desert, and prophets who promised rescue inside the Temple.
verses.fulfilment: Under Felix, deceivers led crowds into the wilderness, and the Egyptian prophet's followers were scattered. On the day the Temple burned in AD 70, about 6,000 people gathered in a Temple portico. A false prophet had promised signs there, and they all died in the fire. After the war, Jonathan the weaver led people into the desert in Cyrene.

evidence.text: Josephus says about 6,000 people died in a burning portico of the Temple, because a false prophet had led them there.
Josephus describes deceivers and the Egyptian prophet leading crowds into the wilderness under Felix.
Josephus says Jonathan, a weaver, led poor people into the desert of Cyrene after the war.

verses.other: Futurist readers apply this to false claims of a secret return of Christ before His visible coming.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that Josephus records exactly these two kinds of deceivers in the years before and during the war.

verses.title: Like lightning from east to west
verses.phrase: as the lightning cometh out of the east
verses.meaning: Jesus says His coming will be like lightning that shines from east to west: sudden, clear and impossible to miss. In the fulfilled reading, His coming here is His coming in judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. It was not hidden in a desert or a room, but seen by all. The Old Testament often pictures God 'coming' in storm and cloud to judge a nation.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 70 Rome's armies destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple. Fulfilled interpreters see this as the visible sign of Christ's judgment, as He told the high priest (Matthew 26:64). Some in this reading add that the Tenth Legion came up from Jericho in the east and camped on the Mount of Olives.

evidence.text: Josephus says the Tenth Legion came by way of Jericho and camped on the Mount of Olives, east of the city.

word.note: In Matthew this word appears only in chapter 24 (verses 3, 27, 37 and 39). It was used for the arrival of a king or official. The fulfilled reading takes it as Christ's presence in judgment on that generation.

verses.other: Futurist readers take this as Christ's visible, bodily return to earth at the end of history, seen by the whole world.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that 'coming on the clouds' is prophetic language for God's judgment (Isaiah 19:1). Jesus told Caiaphas that he would see it.

verses.title: The carcass and the eagles
verses.phrase: wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles
verses.meaning: Jesus says that wherever the carcass is, there the eagles (or vultures) will gather. In the fulfilled reading, the carcass is Jerusalem with its dead Temple system. The eagles are the Roman legions, whose standard was the eagle (aquila). The saying also pictures birds gathering over unburied dead.
verses.fulfilment: In AD 70 the Roman army gathered around Jerusalem and took it. Dead bodies filled the streets and were left unburied. After the Temple burned, the soldiers carried their eagle standards into the Temple court and offered sacrifices to them there.

evidence.text: Josephus says the Romans brought their standards into the Temple court, set them up there and offered sacrifices to them.
Josephus says the lanes of the city were blocked with dead bodies.

word.note: The word can mean an eagle or a vulture, since both gather at dead bodies. Deuteronomy 28:49 warns that a nation will come 'as swift as the eagle' to judge Israel. The Roman legions marched under the eagle standard.

verses.other: Futurist readers take this as a picture of judgment at Christ's return. Some link it to the birds gathering after the battle in Revelation 19:17-18.
verses.answer: The fulfilled reader replies that the eagle was Rome's own emblem. The covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28:49 fits the Roman armies around Jerusalem.

verses.title: Sun, moon and stars go dark
verses.phrase: shall the sun be darkened, and the moon
verses.meaning: The fulfilled reading takes this as the prophets' language for the fall of a ruling power, not the end of the physical universe. Isaiah used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of Babylon, and Ezekiel used them for Egypt. In Genesis the lights 'rule' the day and night, and in Joseph's dream they stand for a family's rulers. So Jesus is saying that the rulers of the old covenant order in Jerusalem would be put out, right after the tribulation of those days.
verses.fulfilment: The collapse of Jerusalem's leadership and Temple order when the city fell to Titus in AD 70, immediately after the siege.

evidence.text: Babylon's fall is described as stars, sun and moon giving no light. Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians, yet the sky did not literally go dark.
God says He will cover the heavens and darken the stars when He puts out Pharaoh, a judgment on Egypt by the king of Babylon.

verses.other: Futurist readers expect literal signs in the sky at Christ's bodily return at the end of history. Others see both a first-century and a final fulfilment.
verses.answer: The same words were used of nations that fell long ago, and no one expects those skies to have gone black. 'Immediately after' ties the signs to the tribulation Jesus had just described.

verses.title: The Son of Man coming on the clouds
verses.phrase: they shall see the Son of man coming
verses.meaning: In the Old Testament, the Lord 'rides on a cloud' when He comes to judge a nation, as in Isaiah 19:1 against Egypt. In this reading, Jesus claims that same role from Daniel 7:13. The 'tribes of the earth' are taken as the tribes of the land of Israel, who mourn (Zechariah 12:10-12). The 'sign' is the judgment itself: the people would see, in the city's fall, that the Son of Man now reigned.
verses.fulfilment: The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, which this reading identifies with the coming (Parousia) of the Son of Man in power.

evidence.text: Jesus told the high priest and council that they would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven.
Josephus reports that before sunset, chariots and armed troops were seen running among the clouds and surrounding the cities (spring AD 66).
Tacitus also records armies seen clashing in the sky and the Temple lit by fire from the clouds.

word.note: The Greek word can mean the whole earth or a particular land. This reading takes 'all the tribes of the ge' as the tribes of Israel's land, as in Zechariah 12:12, where families of the land mourn.

verses.other: Futurist and most historic readers see Christ's visible, bodily return, seen by the whole world. Some partial preterists read verse 30 as AD 70 but keep a future bodily return taught in other texts.
verses.answer: Cloud-coming is God's judgment language in the prophets. Jesus told His own judges that they would see it, so the event fell within their lifetime.

verses.title: The trumpet and the gathering
verses.phrase: he shall send his angels with a great sound
verses.meaning: The Greek angelos means 'messenger', and it is used of human messengers such as John the Baptist (Matthew 11:10). In this reading, the 'angels' are gospel messengers. The great trumpet echoes Isaiah 27:13, where a trumpet calls scattered exiles to worship. Once the old order fell, the elect would be gathered from every direction into the one people of God, the opposite of Jeremiah's scattering of Elam to the four winds.
verses.fulfilment: The gathering of believers from every nation into the church, carried on with new freedom after the Temple system ended in AD 70.

evidence.text: A great trumpet sounds, and those lost in Assyria and Egypt come to worship the Lord at Jerusalem.
Moses promised that God would gather His people even from the farthest part of heaven.

verses.other: Futurist readers see a literal angelic gathering of the elect at Christ's return, either the rapture or the regathering of Israel. Many other readers link it to the final resurrection.
verses.answer: The words 'from one end of heaven to the other' come from Deuteronomy 30:4 and describe a gathering of people, not a trip into the sky. The verse sits within the 'this generation' timeframe of verse 34.

verses.title: The lesson of the fig tree
verses.phrase: Now learn a parable of the fig tree
verses.meaning: Jesus gives a plain lesson from nature. When a fig tree puts out soft leaves, summer is near. In the same way, when the disciples saw the signs He had listed, they would know the end was near. This reading also notes the season. Leaves come in spring, and the siege of Jerusalem began in spring, at Passover. Luke adds 'and all the trees', so the point is the season, not a symbol for a nation.
verses.fulfilment: Titus surrounded Jerusalem in the spring of AD 70, a few days before Passover, when crowds of pilgrims filled the city.

evidence.text: Three legions camped near the city, and the tenth legion camped on the Mount of Olives, where Jesus had spoken.
Josephus says most of the dead had come for the Feast of Unleavened Bread and were shut in by the siege.

verses.other: Many dispensational writers took the fig tree as the modern State of Israel (1948), with the end coming within a generation after that. Others see only a general lesson about reading the signs.
verses.answer: Luke's 'all the trees' shows it is an ordinary picture of the seasons. The lesson was given to the disciples, about signs they themselves would see.

verses.title: Near, even at the doors
verses.phrase: know that it is near, even at the doors
verses.meaning: 'You' means the disciples sitting with Jesus on the Mount of Olives; Mark 13:3 names Peter, James, John and Andrew. When they saw 'all these things', they would know the end was at the door. James, writing to first-century believers, uses the same picture: the Judge is standing at the door. In this reading, the early church heard this as a nearness they would live to see.
verses.fulfilment: The signs of the AD 60s, and above all armies around Jerusalem (Luke 21:20). Cestius Gallus surrounded the city in AD 66 and then withdrew.

evidence.text: James tells his readers that the Judge is standing at the door.
Eusebius says the Jerusalem church was warned by a revelation to leave the city before the war, and settled in Pella.

verses.other: Futurist readers say 'you' means the generation that will see the signs at the end of the age, whoever that may be.
verses.answer: Jesus answered the disciples' own question (Matthew 24:3), so 'you' most naturally means them. The early church acted on the warning and fled.

verses.title: This generation will not pass
verses.phrase: This generation shall not pass
verses.meaning: This is the key time text of the discourse. In Matthew, 'this generation' always means the people living when Jesus spoke (Matthew 11:16; Matthew 23:36). Just a day earlier, Jesus said that all the blood of the prophets would come upon 'this generation'. Jesus said 'this', not 'that'. In Scripture a generation is often about forty years, and the city fell about forty years after He spoke.
verses.fulfilment: Jerusalem and the Temple fell in AD 70, about forty years after Jesus spoke (about AD 30-33).

evidence.text: Jesus says all these things will come upon this generation, speaking to the leaders in front of Him.
Israel wandered forty years until the whole generation that had done evil was gone.
The Temple burned on the tenth of Av, about late August AD 70.

word.gloss: generation; the people alive at one time
word.note: Standard Greek lexicons give the main sense as people born and living at about the same time, 'contemporaries'. A different word, genos, means race or kind. Some futurist notes read genea as 'race' (the Jewish people); preterists answer that the word does not mean that in Matthew.

verses.other: Futurist readers take it as the generation alive when the end-time signs begin, or as the Jewish race surviving until the end. C. S. Lewis called it 'the most embarrassing verse in the Bible'.
verses.answer: In this reading there is nothing embarrassing in it. Jesus said His hearers would see it, and they did. Every other use of 'this generation' in Matthew means His contemporaries.

verses.title: Heaven and earth will pass away
verses.phrase: Heaven and earth shall pass away
verses.meaning: This reading does not take 'heaven and earth' here as the physical universe. It takes it as the covenant world centred on the Temple. Isaiah 51:16 links God's 'planting the heavens' with making Israel His people. Josephus says the parts of the Tabernacle pictured the earth and sea, and heaven. Jesus had said the law would stand 'till heaven and earth pass' (Matthew 5:18). When the Temple fell, the old covenant order passed away, and the Word of Christ remained.
verses.fulfilment: The destruction of the Temple in AD 70 ended the old covenant system of priesthood and sacrifice (Hebrews 8:13).

evidence.text: Josephus says the outer parts of the Tabernacle stood for land and sea, open to people, while the inner room stood for heaven, kept for God.
Written before AD 70, Hebrews says the old covenant is growing old and is ready to vanish away.

word.note: Together the two words can mean the created world. In prophetic speech they can also stand for a covenant order, as when Moses calls heaven and earth to witness (Deuteronomy 32:1). This reading links them to the Temple's holy rooms.

verses.other: Most readers, including many partial preterists, take this as the physical universe, which will end or be renewed at the final judgment. Jesus is contrasting His lasting word with even the most lasting creation.
verses.answer: Matthew 5:18 says not one stroke of the law passes until heaven and earth pass. Hebrews says the old covenant was about to vanish. These fit together if 'heaven and earth' means the covenant world that ended in AD 70.

verses.title: No one knows the day or hour
verses.phrase: But of that day and hour knoweth no man
verses.meaning: Jesus has just given the generation; now He says the exact day and hour are not known. In this reading, these do not conflict. The disciples knew the event would come in their lifetime, but not the day. So they had to stay ready at all times, prepared to leave for the mountains when they saw the signs.
verses.fulfilment: The precise timing of the siege and fall, which came within the generation but at a moment no one could name in advance.

evidence.text: After the resurrection Jesus again told the disciples that times and seasons were in the Father's authority.
The Jerusalem believers left in time, which shows readiness without a fixed date.

verses.other: Many readers see verse 36 as a turn to a different, still-future 'day': the final return of Christ, which has no signs. Others think the whole discourse is about one event.
verses.answer: 'That day' points back to the events just described. Knowing the generation but not the day was exactly the disciples' situation.

verses.title: As in the days of Noah
verses.phrase: as the days of Noe were
verses.meaning: Jesus compares His coming to the flood. In Noah's day God waited while the ark was built, but the people did not repent, and judgment came on that generation. In this reading, God gave Jerusalem about forty years after the cross to hear the gospel. When most leaders refused, judgment came on that generation too, just as it came on Noah's.
verses.fulfilment: The judgment of AD 70, which this reading identifies with the Parousia, after about forty years of gospel preaching in Judea.

evidence.text: Peter says God waited patiently in Noah's day while the ark was built, and only eight people were saved.
God set a limit of one hundred and twenty years before the flood.

word.note: The word was used for the visit of a king or official to a city. It appears in Matthew only in this chapter (24:3, 27, 37, 39). This reading takes it as Christ's coming in judgment on Jerusalem.

verses.other: Futurist readers see the days of Noah as a picture of the world just before Christ's bodily return, with people living normally and unprepared.
verses.answer: Noah's flood was a judgment on one generation. Jesus applies it to 'this generation', so the comparison fits the end of Jerusalem's age.

verses.title: Eating, drinking, marrying
verses.phrase: eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage
verses.meaning: Life went on as normal before the flood. In this reading, life in Jerusalem also went on as normal after the cross. The priests kept offering daily sacrifices, as if the final sacrifice had not been made. Hebrews says the old system was a copy and a shadow. Daily routine hid the danger, and few saw that the old covenant age was ending.
verses.fulfilment: Temple worship continued until the daily sacrifice stopped during the siege in summer AD 70, shortly before the Temple burned.

evidence.text: Josephus records that the daily sacrifice failed on the seventeenth of Tammuz (July AD 70) for lack of men to offer it.
The way into the holy place was not yet open while the first tabernacle was still standing.

verses.other: Futurist readers apply this to the general spirit of the world before Christ returns: carelessness rather than open wickedness.
verses.answer: Jesus was speaking about His hearers' own world. In Jerusalem the normal routine included Temple sacrifices that continued until the siege.

verses.title: The flood took them all away
verses.phrase: the flood came, and took them all away
verses.meaning: This is a key point in the fulfilled reading. In the flood, the people who were 'taken away' were the wicked, swept away in judgment. Noah and his family were the ones left. So in this picture, being taken is not a rescue. It means being removed in judgment, just as Jerusalem's rebels were removed in AD 70.
verses.fulfilment: The killing and capture of Jerusalem's population in AD 70.

evidence.text: Josephus counts 97,000 people taken captive during the whole war and gives a very large number of dead.
Every living thing was wiped out; only Noah and those with him in the ark were left.

verses.other: Many futurist readers agree that the flood 'took away' the wicked, but see this as the world's judgment at Christ's return.
verses.answer: In the flood the wicked were removed and the righteous remained. That pattern happened to Jerusalem within the generation.

verses.title: Two in the field
verses.phrase: the one shall be taken, and the other left
verses.meaning: Following verse 39, this reading takes 'taken' as taken in judgment, like the flood. Farm workers out in the open fields were exposed when the Roman army arrived. Some were seized as captives, and others escaped. Jesus warns that people side by side could meet very different ends. Rome often took captives as slaves.
verses.fulfilment: The Roman army swept through Judea from AD 67 to 70, killing and capturing people across the countryside.

evidence.text: After the fall, captives over seventeen were sent in chains to work in Egypt, and many were sent to the provinces to die in arenas.
Josephus counts 97,000 captives in the war.

word.gloss: to take along, to take with oneself
word.note: Verse 39 uses a different verb for the flood 'taking away' (airo). Futurist readers note that paralambano is used in John 14:3 for Christ 'receiving' His people. Preterists answer that context, the flood parallel, decides the meaning.

verses.other: Pre-tribulation readers often see the rapture here: believers taken to Christ, unbelievers left. Others take it as the separation at Christ's return.
verses.answer: Jesus has just said the flood 'took them all away'. In that picture the ones taken are the ones judged. Luke 17:37 adds that the taken go where the vultures gather.

verses.title: Two women at the mill
verses.phrase: Two women shall be grinding at the mill
verses.meaning: Grinding grain for bread was daily work for women in every home. In this reading, Jesus warns that ordinary work would not protect anyone when the army came. Women, like men, could be taken as captives. The disciples were to make sure their families stayed alert and ready to flee.
verses.fulfilment: The capture and sale of women and children when Jerusalem and the towns of Judea fell (AD 67-70).

evidence.text: Josephus says the Romans sold the people, with their wives and children, at a very low price because there were so many.
After Jerusalem's first fall, young men were forced to grind at the mill.

verses.other: Futurist readers see the sudden separation of believers and unbelievers at Christ's coming, in the middle of ordinary life.
verses.answer: The setting is a village of first-century Judea, and the warning is to flee in time. The judgment that came was the Roman war.

verses.title: Watch
verses.phrase: ye know not what hour your Lord doth come
verses.meaning: Because the hour was not known, the disciples had to keep watch. In this reading, this is practical advice about real danger. About forty years would pass, and by then the disciples would have families and churches to protect. Watching meant staying faithful in the mission while being ready to act on Jesus' warning.
verses.fulfilment: The Jerusalem church's flight before the war, which this reading sees as obedience to the call to watch.

evidence.text: The believers in Jerusalem left the city before the war and went to Pella in Perea.
Jesus told them to watch and pray, so that they could escape what was about to happen.

verses.other: Most Christians apply this to every generation, which should live ready for Christ's return at any time.
verses.answer: The command was first for the disciples facing a real war. Its lesson of faithful readiness still applies to all believers.

verses.title: The thief in the night
verses.phrase: if the goodman of the house had known
verses.meaning: A thief does not announce when he will come. In this reading, the coming judgment would break in like a thief, and the Roman army would arrive on the city suddenly. The owner who watches is not caught. The disciples were to live normally but keep watch.
verses.fulfilment: Titus arrived just before Passover in AD 70, and the pilgrims who had come for the feast were trapped inside the walls.

evidence.text: Josephus explains that the crowds had come from the whole country for the feast and were suddenly shut in by the war.
Jesus warns a first-century church that He will come like a thief if they do not watch.

verses.other: Futurist readers see Christ's return coming suddenly on an unready world. Paul's 'thief' language is often read the same way.
verses.answer: Paul told the Thessalonians that the day would not surprise them, because they were children of light. The warning was for people who could live to see it.

verses.title: Be ready
verses.phrase: Therefore be ye also ready
verses.meaning: This reading asks who is speaking and to whom. Jesus speaks to Peter, James, John and Andrew. 'You also be ready' was a call to them. They did not know the hour, but they knew it would come within their lifetime. The Son of Man would come when they did not expect, so readiness had to be constant.
verses.fulfilment: The judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, within the lifetime of the disciples who heard the warning.

evidence.text: Mark names the four listeners: Peter, James, John and Andrew.
When they saw Jerusalem surrounded by armies, they would know its desolation was near.

verses.other: Futurist readers see a timeless call for all believers to be ready for Christ's bodily return, whenever it may come.
verses.answer: The call was first a life-saving warning for the disciples' own generation. Readiness and faithfulness remain the lesson for us.

verses.title: The faithful and wise servant
verses.phrase: Who then is a faithful and wise servant
verses.meaning: Jesus now turns from warning to stewardship. The servant set over the household gives food at the right time. In this reading, the servants are the apostles and leaders of the first church, who had to feed God's people through about forty hard years before the end came. Jesus later called them friends, not only servants.
verses.fulfilment: The apostolic ministry from Pentecost (about AD 30-33) to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.

evidence.text: Jesus tells Peter to feed His sheep.
Paul says stewards must be found faithful.

verses.other: Futurist and most other readers apply the servant to all church leaders and believers in every age until Christ returns.
verses.answer: The parable first addressed the apostles, who were left in charge until the Master came within their generation. Every steward can still learn from it.

verses.title: Blessed when the master comes
verses.phrase: Blessed is that servant, whom his lord when he cometh
verses.meaning: The servant who is found faithful at the master's coming is blessed. In this reading, Jesus encourages His disciples, as a group and one by one, to keep going until His coming. The blessing goes to the one who keeps on working, not to the one who guesses the date. This leads into the parables of Matthew 25.
verses.fulfilment: The faithful believers who kept serving through the persecutions and wars of AD 30-70.

evidence.text: Jesus tells a first-century church to be faithful until death and promises the crown of life.
Paul, near the end of his life, says he has finished the race and kept the faith.

verses.other: Most readers see a blessing for every faithful believer when Christ returns at the end of history.
verses.answer: The promise was to people who would see the coming in their lifetime. The principle of faithful service is the same today.

verses.title: Ruler over all his goods
verses.phrase: he shall make him ruler over all his goods
verses.meaning: The reward for faithful service is greater responsibility. In this reading, the faithful servants share in Christ's rule. Jesus promised the Twelve that they would sit on thrones in the 'regeneration'. Some interpreters link this to the original call to have dominion in Genesis 1:28, now given to the church.
verses.fulfilment: The church's place in Christ's kingdom after the old covenant order passed away in AD 70.

evidence.text: Jesus gives His disciples a kingdom, as the Father gave one to Him.
The one who overcomes will sit with Christ on His throne.

verses.other: Futurist readers place the reward in the future, for example ruling with Christ in a millennial kingdom after His return.
verses.answer: Jesus said the Twelve would judge Israel 'in the regeneration'. This reading sees that new order as beginning when the old covenant age ended.

verses.title: My lord delays his coming
verses.phrase: My lord delayeth his coming
verses.meaning: Jesus calls the servant who says 'my master is delaying' evil. In this reading, the fault is to treat the coming as far off and so to live carelessly. Some preterists also see a warning against speaking as if Christ's promise to come within that generation had failed.
verses.fulfilment: Scoffers in the decades before AD 70 who asked, 'Where is the promise of His coming?'

evidence.text: Peter warns of scoffers who ask where the promise of His coming is.
Hebrews says that in a very little while the coming one will come and will not delay.

verses.other: Many readers note that the parable itself assumes some delay (compare Matthew 25:5, 19). The evil servant's sin is misusing the delay, not expecting one.
verses.answer: Hebrews promised that He would not delay. In this reading the delay was short, within a generation, and the servant's mistake was to think it long.

verses.title: Beating fellow servants
verses.phrase: shall begin to smite his fellowservants
verses.meaning: The evil servant turns on his fellow servants and joins the drunkards. In this reading, the picture fits the years before AD 70. Jerusalem's leaders persecuted the church. Later the city's own factions fought and killed one another. Instead of feeding the household, its leaders wounded it.
verses.fulfilment: Persecution of Jerusalem's believers (AD 30-62) and the civil war between the factions inside the city (AD 67-70).

evidence.text: The high priest Ananus had James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in AD 62.
The rival leaders John and Simon fought each other and burned the city's grain stores, which led to famine.

verses.other: Most readers see a picture of any unfaithful leader in the church who abuses others and lives for pleasure while waiting for Christ.
verses.answer: Matthew 23:34 has just said that Jerusalem's leaders would beat and kill Jesus' messengers. This verse fits that warning.

verses.title: An hour he is not aware of
verses.phrase: shall come in a day when he looketh not
verses.meaning: The careless servant is caught by surprise. In this reading, the master's coming matched the Roman army's arrival, which came on people who were still sure of rescue. Many expected God to deliver the city even as it burned, and they had no way out.
verses.fulfilment: The fall of the Temple and city in AD 70, when many still expected rescue until the end.

evidence.text: A false prophet told the people to go up to the Temple to receive signs of deliverance; about 6,000 died when the portico burned.
Tacitus says many Jews believed ancient writings foretold that men from Judea would rule the world at that very time.

verses.other: Futurist readers see the sudden return of Christ catching unfaithful professing believers unprepared.
verses.answer: The people of Jerusalem looked for rescue, not judgment. Jesus warned that the master's coming would surprise those who were not watching.
