verses.title: Cut asunder, with the hypocrites
verses.phrase: shall cut him asunder, and appoint him his portion
verses.meaning: The punishment is severe: the servant is 'cut in two' and given a place with the hypocrites. In Matthew 23 Jesus called the scribes and Pharisees 'hypocrites' seven times. So in this reading, the evil servant shares the fate of Jerusalem's leaders. Weeping and gnashing of teeth is what Jesus had said would happen to 'the sons of the kingdom' who were cast out.
verses.fulfilment: The destruction of Jerusalem's leadership in AD 70.

evidence.text: Jesus begins a series of woes on the scribes and Pharisees, calling them hypocrites.
The sons of the kingdom will be thrown out, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

word.note: The word is used in the Greek Old Testament for cutting up a sacrifice (Exodus 29:17). Some take it literally as a cruel death; others take it as being cut off, severely punished. Hypokrites first meant a stage actor, someone playing a part.

verses.other: Most readers see final judgment on false or unfaithful believers when Christ returns.
verses.answer: Jesus links the evil servant to the 'hypocrites' He had just judged in Matthew 23, and that judgment was to fall on 'this generation'.

verses.title: The ten virgins
verses.phrase: Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him
verses.meaning: There were no chapter breaks in Matthew, so this parable continues the same talk to the same disciples. The bridegroom is Jesus. Some interpreters take the lamp as God's word and the oil as the Holy Spirit. The point is readiness: wise people prepare for a delay, but foolish people do not. In this reading, the wedding is the union of Christ and His church, completed when the old covenant age ended.
verses.fulfilment: The coming of the Bridegroom, which this reading places at AD 70, after a 'delay' of about forty years.

evidence.text: The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready.
Jesus had just told a parable of a king's wedding feast, ending with the city of the murderers burned.

verses.other: Futurist readers see believers or Israel needing readiness for Christ's return. Many apply the 'shut door' to the final judgment.
verses.answer: The parable ends with the same call as Matthew 24:42, 'Watch', and so it shares that chapter's timeframe.

verses.title: The talents
verses.phrase: After a long time the lord of those servants cometh
verses.meaning: A master entrusts money to his servants and returns 'after a long time' to settle accounts. Two servants trade and double what they were given. The third hides his talent out of fear. In this reading, the long time is the forty years before AD 70. The servants who received the kingdom had to make it bear fruit, while the old order lost what it had.
verses.fulfilment: The accounting at AD 70, when the kingdom was taken from the unfruitful and given to a fruitful people (Matthew 21:43).

evidence.text: Jesus told the leaders that the kingdom would be taken from them and given to a people who bear its fruit.
Luke's similar parable was told because the people thought the kingdom would appear at once.

verses.other: Most readers apply the parable to all believers, who will give account at Christ's return for how they used His gifts.
verses.answer: The 'long time' is long for a lifetime, not for twenty centuries. The parable follows the same 'watch' teaching aimed at the disciples' generation.

verses.title: The sheep and the goats
verses.phrase: When the Son of man shall come in his glory
verses.meaning: The Son of Man comes in glory with His angels and sits on His throne. He gathers the nations and separates them. Jesus had already said He would come in glory and reward each person while some of His hearers still lived (Matthew 16:27-28). In this reading, the scene shows Christ's reign over all nations beginning with the judgment on Jerusalem. The 'least of these' are His messengers (Matthew 10:42).
verses.fulfilment: The judgment of AD 70 and the kingdom opened to all nations. Full preterists place the whole scene there; partial preterists place it at a final judgment.

evidence.text: The Son of Man will come in His Father's glory with His angels and reward each person by what they have done.
Some standing there would not taste death before they saw the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.

verses.other: Most Christians, including partial preterists, see the final judgment of all people at the end of history, since verse 46 speaks of eternal life and eternal punishment.
verses.answer: The same 'coming in glory with angels' was promised within His hearers' lifetime. In this reading the judgment that began then has eternal results.

symbols.image: The sun darkened, the moon without light, the stars falling
symbols.meaning: The prophets used this picture when a ruling power fell. Isaiah used it for the fall of Babylon, and Ezekiel used it for the fall of Egypt. In Joseph's dream the sun, moon and stars stood for his family, so they can stand for rulers. The fulfilled reading takes the verse as the collapse of Jerusalem's ruling order in AD 70, not as a failure of the physical sky.

symbols.image: The Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven
symbols.meaning: In the Old Testament God "rides on a cloud" when He comes to judge a nation, as He did against Egypt. No one saw God's body in those events. They saw His judgment in history. The fulfilled reading holds that Jesus claimed this divine role before the high priest, and that His generation saw it when Rome destroyed the city and temple.

This reading takes "heaven and earth" as covenant and temple language, not the physical universe. Josephus says the tabernacle was laid out as a picture of the world: the parts open to the priests stood for land and sea, and the inner room stood for heaven (Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7). Some interpreters therefore map the Holy of Holies to heaven, the Holy Place to earth and the outer court to sea, and they hold that this "world" passed away when the temple fell. Jesus' words, by contrast, would remain.

symbols.image: The abomination of desolation standing in the holy place
symbols.meaning: Daniel speaks of a defiling thing that stops the sacrifices and leaves the sanctuary desolate. Luke's parallel explains it plainly: Jerusalem surrounded by armies. The fulfilled reading sees the Roman armies, with their idol-like standards, as the defiling power. Some also include the Zealots, who turned the temple into a fortress and shed blood in its courts (Josephus, Jewish War 4.3.7-10).

symbols.image: Where the carcass is, there the eagles gather
symbols.meaning: The Greek word can mean eagle or vulture. Literally, the dead of the siege lay unburied for the birds. Symbolically, the eagle was the emblem on the Roman legions' standards, and Moses had warned of a nation "like an eagle" coming against a disobedient Israel. Josephus records that the soldiers set up their standards in the temple court and sacrificed to them while the temple burned (Josephus, Jewish War 6.6.1).

symbols.image: Lightning flashing from east to west
symbols.meaning: The point of the picture is that His coming would be public and impossible to miss. It would not be hidden in the desert or in secret rooms, where false messiahs gathered followers. In the Psalms lightning goes with God's coming in judgment. Some fulfilled-reading writers add a geographical link to the Roman advance, but that detail is debated; the main point is visibility and speed.

symbols.image: The fig tree putting out leaves
symbols.meaning: Leaves on a fig tree show that summer is near. In the same way, the signs Jesus listed would show the disciples that the city's fall was near, so they could leave in time. Luke says "the fig tree and all the trees", so this reading takes it as an ordinary seasonal lesson, not a code for a modern nation. Some also recall the barren fig tree Jesus cursed in Matthew 21 as a picture of a fruitless temple system.

symbols.image: A great trumpet and the gathering of the elect from the four winds
symbols.meaning: In Israel trumpets called the people to gather, and Isaiah speaks of a great trumpet that brings the scattered home to worship. The Greek word for angels also means messengers. The fulfilled reading takes the verse as the gospel call going out through God's messengers, gathering His people from every nation into the new covenant community once the old order fell.

symbols.image: As in the days of Noah
symbols.meaning: Noah's neighbours went on eating, drinking and marrying, and ignored the warning until the flood came. God had waited patiently before the flood. This reading sees a parallel in the roughly forty years between Jesus' warning and AD 70. In the flood it was the wicked who were "taken away", so this reading takes "one taken" as taken in judgment, such as captured by Rome, not rescued.

symbols.image: The thief who comes at an unknown hour
symbols.meaning: A thief does not announce the hour he will come, so the owner must stay awake. The picture stresses that the exact time was unknown, even though the generation was known. The fulfilled reading applies it to the believers of that generation, who had to stay ready to flee at short notice. Paul and Revelation use the same picture for a coming their first readers had to watch for.

In Jewish custom a betrothal came first, and then, after a waiting time, the groom came to take his bride home. Jesus called Himself the bridegroom. Some fulfilled-reading writers see the years between the cross and AD 70 as that waiting time, ending when Christ came for His bride, the church, as the old covenant passed. The lamps and oil call for faithful readiness through a dark and long night.

symbols.image: The shepherd separating the sheep from the goats
symbols.meaning: Ezekiel pictures God as a shepherd who judges between sheep and goats among His own flock. The King gathers "all the nations", which shows that the kingdom is no longer limited to Israel. Here fulfilled readers differ. Full preterists place this judgment at the coming in AD 70, while partial preterists, with most churches, read it as the final judgment still to come.

The Greek word aion means an age or era, not the physical world. The fulfilled reading takes the disciples' question as asking about the end of the Mosaic covenant age, which they linked with the temple's fall. New Testament writers spoke of their own time as the end of the ages, and Hebrews describes the old covenant as about to vanish.

The word for sorrows means labour pains. Pain in labour grows stronger, but it leads to new life. This reading sees the wars, famines and earthquakes before AD 70 as the pains that came before the new covenant age was fully born. Paul and the prophets use the same picture for the birth of a new people.

timeTexts.phrase: till the Son of man be come
timeTexts.note: Jesus told the Twelve they would not finish going through the towns of Israel before the Son of Man came. The fulfilled reading takes this as a coming within their working lives.

timeTexts.phrase: some standing here, which shall not taste of death
timeTexts.note: The coming with angels to repay each person is tied to the lifetime of some who heard Him. Others read verse 28 as the Transfiguration, the resurrection or Pentecost.

timeTexts.phrase: All these things shall come upon this generation
timeTexts.note: Spoken to the leaders in the temple, just before the discourse. It sets the time frame that Matthew 24:34 repeats.

timeTexts.phrase: This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled
timeTexts.note: The central time text of the discourse. The fulfilled reading takes 'this generation' as Jesus' own contemporaries.

timeTexts.phrase: Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man
timeTexts.note: Jesus told the high priest and the council that they themselves would see Him seated at God's right hand and coming on the clouds.

timeTexts.phrase: The night is far spent, the day is at hand
timeTexts.note: Paul tells the Roman church that their salvation is nearer than when they first believed.

timeTexts.phrase: shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly
timeTexts.note: A promise of victory to the believers in Rome, described as coming soon.
Paul advises the Corinthians in light of the shortened time and says the present form of this world is passing away.

timeTexts.phrase: upon whom the ends of the world are come
timeTexts.note: The Greek speaks of the ends of the ages. Paul places his own generation at the close of the ages.
Some read this as nearness in time, others as nearness in presence. The fulfilled reading takes it as time.

timeTexts.phrase: he that shall come will come, and will not tarry
timeTexts.note: Drawing on Habakkuk 2:3, the writer tells suffering believers that the coming One will arrive in a very little while.

timeTexts.phrase: the coming of the Lord draweth nigh
timeTexts.note: James adds that the Judge is standing at the door. The fulfilled reading links this to the judgment on Jerusalem.

timeTexts.phrase: the end of all things is at hand
timeTexts.note: Peter urges sober prayer because the end is near. The fulfilled reading takes 'all things' as the old covenant order.

timeTexts.phrase: Little children, it is the last time
timeTexts.note: John says that many antichrists have already appeared, and that this shows it is the last hour.

timeTexts.phrase: things which must shortly come to pass
timeTexts.note: The book opens by saying its events must happen soon. The fulfilled reading stresses that this covers all of them, not only some.

timeTexts.phrase: for the time is at hand
timeTexts.note: A blessing on those who read and keep the prophecy, because the time is near.

timeTexts.phrase: Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book
timeTexts.note: John must not seal his book because the time is near. Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4).
The last promise in the Bible. Futurist readers take 'quickly' as sudden or certain; the fulfilled reading takes it as soon.

timeline.label: Jesus foretells the temple's fall
timeline.text: On the Mount of Olives, in the last week before the cross (about AD 30, or AD 33 on another dating), Jesus tells four disciples that not one stone of the temple will be left on another. He adds that this generation will not pass away before it happens.

timeline.label: Pentecost
timeline.text: Fifty days after the resurrection the Spirit comes on the disciples in Jerusalem. Jews "from every nation under heaven" hear the gospel, and the message begins to spread across the Roman world (Acts 2).

timeline.label: Stephen is stoned
timeline.text: Stephen is put to death in Jerusalem (Acts 7), probably in the early or middle 30s. A wide persecution follows, and believers scatter through Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1).

timeline.label: James son of Zebedee is killed
timeline.text: King Herod Agrippa I has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword and arrests Peter (Acts 12:1-3). Agrippa dies the same year.

timeline.label: Theudas leads people to the Jordan
timeline.text: Under the governor Fadus (AD 44-46), Theudas claims to be a prophet and promises to part the Jordan. Roman cavalry kill many of his followers (Josephus, Antiquities 20.5.1; compare Acts 5:36).

timeline.label: Famine under Claudius
timeline.text: Agabus had foretold a great famine over "all the world", and it came in the days of Claudius (Acts 11:28). Judea suffered badly around AD 46-48 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.2.5 and 20.5.2). The church in Antioch sent relief to Judea (Acts 11:29-30).

timeline.label: Paul before Gallio at Corinth
timeline.text: On his mission across the Roman world, Paul is brought before Gallio, governor of Achaia (Acts 18:12-17). An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio's term to about AD 51-52, which helps fix the timeline of Paul's travels.

timeline.label: The Egyptian false prophet
timeline.text: Under the governor Felix, a man called "the Egyptian" gathers followers on the Mount of Olives and promises that the walls of Jerusalem will fall. Felix scatters them (Josephus, Jewish War 2.13.5; compare Acts 21:38).

timeline.label: The gospel heard "in all the world"
timeline.text: Writing to Rome around AD 57, Paul says the Romans' faith is reported in all the world (Romans 1:8). A few years later he says the gospel has been preached to every creature under heaven (Colossians 1:23).

timeline.label: Earthquakes in Asia and Italy
timeline.text: Laodicea is ruined by an earthquake and rebuilds without Roman help (Tacitus, Annals 14.27, AD 60). In AD 62 an earthquake strikes Pompeii in Campania (Tacitus, Annals 15.22; Seneca, Natural Questions 6.1). Seneca was Gallio's brother.

timeline.label: James the Just is killed
timeline.text: Between two Roman governors, the high priest Ananus has James, the brother of Jesus, and others stoned in Jerusalem (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9.1).

timeline.label: Nero's persecution in Rome
timeline.text: After the great fire of July AD 64, Nero blames the Christians. Some are arrested and inform on many others. Victims are torn by dogs, crucified, or burned as torches at night (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Christian tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Nero's reign.

timeline.label: The Jewish revolt begins
timeline.text: Riots follow the governor Florus' seizure of temple money. The priests stop the daily sacrifice offered for the emperor, which Josephus calls the start of the war (Josephus, Jewish War 2.17.2). Factions also fight one another.

timeline.label: Cestius Gallus withdraws; flight to Pella
timeline.text: In November AD 66 the Syrian governor Cestius Gallus attacks Jerusalem, then suddenly withdraws and is routed at Beth-horon (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19.7-9). Eusebius says the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left the city before the war and settled in Pella beyond the Jordan (Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3). Many see this pause as the signal Luke 21:20-21 describes.

timeline.label: Vespasian takes command
timeline.text: Nero sends Vespasian with his son Titus. In AD 67 they subdue Galilee, and Josephus himself is captured at Jotapata (Josephus, Jewish War 3.7).

timeline.label: Nero dies
timeline.text: Vespasian takes much of Judea and Peraea. Nero dies in June AD 68, and Vespasian pauses the campaign while Rome falls into turmoil (Suetonius, Nero 49; Josephus, Jewish War 4.9.2).

timeline.label: The year of four emperors
timeline.text: Galba, Otho and Vitellius rise and fall in quick succession. In July AD 69 the eastern legions proclaim Vespasian emperor, and he wins (Tacitus, Histories 2.79-81; Suetonius, Vespasian 6). Inside Jerusalem, rival factions fight each other.

timeline.label: Titus begins the siege at Passover
timeline.text: In spring AD 70, shortly before Passover, Titus camps before Jerusalem with four legions, one of them on the Mount of Olives (Josephus, Jewish War 5.2.3 and 5.3.1). Pilgrims crowd the city, and famine soon follows (Jewish War 5.12.3; 6.3.4).

timeline.label: The Antonia fortress falls
timeline.text: In July AD 70 Roman troops take the Antonia fortress beside the temple by a night attack, and Titus orders it torn down to open a way to the temple courts (Josephus, Jewish War 6.1.7-8 and 6.2.1).

timeline.label: The daily sacrifice ceases
timeline.text: On the 17th of Panemus, in mid-summer AD 70, the daily sacrifice fails for lack of men to offer it (Josephus, Jewish War 6.2.1). Many readers link this with Daniel's words about the sacrifice being taken away (Daniel 9:27; 12:11).

timeline.label: The temple burns
timeline.text: On the 10th of Lous, the same day as the Babylonian burning (9/10 Av, about late August AD 70), a soldier throws a burning brand into the temple and it is destroyed (Josephus, Jewish War 6.4.5-8). The soldiers then set up their eagle standards in the court and sacrifice to them (Jewish War 6.6.1).

timeline.label: The upper city falls
timeline.text: On the 8th of Gorpiaeus (September AD 70) the upper city is taken and the whole city falls (Josephus, Jewish War 6.8.5). Josephus counts 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead during the war and siege (Jewish War 6.9.3). Titus orders the city and temple razed, leaving only three towers and part of the wall (Jewish War 7.1.1).

timeline.label: Triumph in Rome
timeline.text: Vespasian and Titus celebrate a triumph in Rome. The golden table and the lampstand from the temple are carried in the procession (Josephus, Jewish War 7.5.5). The Arch of Titus, set up after his death in AD 81, still shows the scene.

timeline.label: Masada falls
timeline.text: The last rebel stronghold, Masada by the Dead Sea, falls to the Roman governor Flavius Silva in AD 73 or 74. Josephus says the defenders took their own lives rather than be captured (Josephus, Jewish War 7.8-9).

doubleFulfilment.text: 'Double fulfilment' is the idea that a prophecy can be fulfilled twice: once in the first century, and again on a larger scale at the end of history. Many futurist and some other readers apply this to Matthew 24. They accept that AD 70 fulfilled part of it, but expect a second and greater fulfilment before Christ returns. The fulfilled reading rejects this for Matthew 24. It holds that Jesus gave one prophecy, with one time limit, to one generation, and that it was fulfilled once. It also has a practical concern. If believers expect a repeat, they may wait in fear for disaster instead of serving Christ with confidence now.

points.title: Sealed for later, unsealed for now
points.text: Daniel was told to seal up his vision because it referred to many days in the future, until 'the time of the end'. John was told the opposite: do not seal the prophecy, because the time is near. The fulfilled reading sees Revelation as the opening of what Daniel sealed. On this view, the 'time of the end' is the end of Israel's old covenant age, not the end of time, and it had arrived in John's day.

points.title: One generation, one time limit
points.text: Jesus said that 'this generation' would not pass away until all these things happened. He did not say that some things would happen then and the rest later. The same phrase in Matthew 23:36 clearly means the people He was speaking to. A second fulfilment, the reading argues, would need a second time limit, and the text gives none.

points.title: A tribulation that cannot happen again
points.text: Jesus said the great tribulation would be worse than anything before it 'or ever shall be'. If it can never be equalled, the reading argues, it cannot be repeated on a larger scale later. It happened once, in the disciples' generation.

points.title: The temple and its system are gone
points.text: The prophecy is tied to a particular building, city and land: the holy place, Judea, Sabbath travel and flat housetops. Hebrews says the old covenant was becoming obsolete and ready to vanish away. The fulfilled reading holds that God's dwelling is now His people, so there is no need for another temple to be defiled or destroyed.

points.title: Once, at the end of the ages
points.text: Christ appeared once at the end of the ages to put away sin. The great saving events, His birth, death, resurrection and the giving of the Spirit, are not repeated. The fulfilled reading places the close of the old covenant age with these once-for-all events. Paul could say that the ends of the ages had come on his own generation.

doubleFulfilment.otherSide: Those who hold to multiple or typological fulfilment make a serious case. First, prophecy often has near and far horizons. Isaiah 7:14 had a sign for King Ahaz, yet Matthew 1:23 sees its fullest meaning in Jesus. Joel 2 was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-21), but its signs in the sun and moon may also point further. Second, the 'abomination of desolation' itself shows a pattern. Daniel's words were first fulfilled when Antiochus IV defiled the temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54), yet Jesus applied them to a later event. If one prophecy can be fulfilled more than once, the same may be true of Jesus' own words. Third, some features of the discourse seem wider than AD 70: the coming like lightning seen from east to west, the gathering of the elect from the four winds, and the final judgment of all nations in Matthew 25:31-46. Fourth, Luke speaks of Jerusalem trampled 'until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled' (Luke 21:24), which suggests a long period after AD 70. Many partial preterists and amillennial readers see AD 70 as a real, God-given preview of the final judgment, a type of the last day rather than its replacement. For them, the fall of Jerusalem shows how certainly Christ's final coming will also arrive.

revelationDate.title: John's age
revelationDate.argument: John is told he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations and kings (Revelation 10:11). Early-date writers argue that this fits a man in his sixties, writing in the late 60s, better than a man past ninety in AD 95-96.
revelationDate.counter: Late-date scholars reply that the verse may mean John's written prophecy would reach the nations, not that he would travel. Early church writers also describe John working in Ephesus as a very old man, into the reign of Trajan (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4; Clement of Alexandria, Who Is the Rich Man 42).

revelationDate.title: The seven churches
revelationDate.argument: Revelation is written to seven real churches in Asia (Revelation 1:4). Some early-date writers argue that this list fits the 60s, after an earthquake struck Laodicea and its neighbours, Colossae and Hierapolis, around AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27). The coming "hour of trial" (Revelation 3:10) would then be the Neronian persecution and the war that followed.
revelationDate.counter: Late-date scholars note that seven is a number of completeness in Revelation, and that other churches in Asia existed at the time (Acts 20:5; Colossians 4:13). Laodicea rebuilt quickly and is called rich (Revelation 3:17). Polycarp's letter may suggest that the church at Smyrna did not yet exist when Paul wrote (Polycarp, Philippians 11.3), and Ephesus has lost its first love (Revelation 2:4). They take both points as signs of a later date.

revelationDate.title: The temple still standing
revelationDate.argument: John is told to measure the temple and altar, while the outer court is given to the nations to trample for forty-two months (Revelation 11:1-2). Early-date writers argue that this assumes the Jerusalem temple still stood. It matches Jesus' words that Jerusalem would be trampled by the Gentiles (Luke 21:24), and no New Testament text speaks of a rebuilt temple.
revelationDate.counter: Late-date scholars answer that this is a vision, like Ezekiel's measured temple, which was given when the temple lay in ruins (Ezekiel 40:1-3). In Revelation the temple often stands for God's people (Revelation 3:12). A symbolic temple does not need a standing building.

revelationDate.title: The tribes of the earth
revelationDate.argument: Revelation 1:7 says that those who pierced Him will see Him coming with the clouds, and the tribes of the earth will mourn. This joins Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10, the same texts behind Matthew 24:30. The apostles laid the guilt of the crucifixion on Jerusalem's leaders of that generation (Acts 2:36; 1 Thessalonians 2:14-15), and the Greek word for earth can mean the land. So early-date writers take the book's theme to be a coming in judgment on that generation, which would only make sense before AD 70.
revelationDate.counter: Late-date scholars note that Revelation adds "every eye" and often uses "tribes" and "earth" for all peoples (Revelation 5:9; 7:9). They also note that the verse tells us the book's theme, not the year it was written.

revelationDate.title: The woman and the great city
revelationDate.argument: The great city is "where also their Lord was crucified" (Revelation 11:8). Babylon is drunk with the blood of the saints and prophets (Revelation 17:6; 18:24), the same blood-guilt Jesus laid on Jerusalem (Matthew 23:35-37). The prophets had called Jerusalem "Sodom" (Isaiah 1:10). So early-date writers identify Babylon as Jerusalem, judged in AD 70.
revelationDate.counter: Many scholars point out that the woman sits on seven hills and rules over the kings of the earth (Revelation 17:9, 17:18), which fits Rome. After AD 70 Jewish writers used "Babylon" as a name for Rome because Rome, like Babylon, had destroyed the temple (4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, Sibylline Oracles 5). Late-date scholars take this naming as a sign that Revelation was written after AD 70.

revelationDate.title: The sixth king: Nero
revelationDate.argument: Five kings have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come and will remain a short time (Revelation 17:10). Counting from Julius Caesar, as Suetonius and Josephus do, the five are Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius and Claudius. The sixth, who "is", would be Nero (AD 54-68), and the short seventh would be Galba, who ruled about seven months. On this count John wrote while Nero reigned.
revelationDate.counter: Others begin with Augustus, or skip the three short reigns of AD 68-69, which can lead to Vespasian or Domitian. Many take the seven kings as a symbol of the whole line of world empires. Many late-date scholars also link the beast who "was, and is not" (Revelation 17:8, 17:11) to the legend that Nero would return, which spread after his death.

revelationDate.title: The song of Moses
revelationDate.argument: Those who overcome the beast sing the song of Moses (Revelation 15:3). Early-date writers link this to Deuteronomy 32, a song about Israel in the latter days, about a perverse generation and about God avenging the blood of His servants (Deuteronomy 31:29; 32:5, 32:43). The martyrs' cry for vengeance (Revelation 6:10) fits the blood-guilt laid on Jesus' generation (Matthew 23:35). So the martyrs would be first-century believers.
revelationDate.counter: Late-date scholars note that the words of the song in Revelation 15:3-4 praise God's works and say all nations will come and worship. That echoes the song of deliverance in Exodus 15 more than the judgment song of Deuteronomy 32. A song of Moses can suit persecuted believers in any period.

revelationDate.title: The time element
revelationDate.argument: Revelation says its events "must shortly come to pass" and that "the time is at hand" (Revelation 1:1, 1:3; 22:6, 22:10). Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far off (Daniel 8:26; 12:4), but John is told not to seal his. Early-date writers argue that the nearness covers the whole book and points to the fall of Jerusalem.
revelationDate.counter: Futurists often read "shortly" as "swiftly once it begins", or measure it by God's time (2 Peter 3:8). Late-date scholars also note that nearness does not fix a date, since a book written in AD 95 could expect near events in Rome. They rely on the testimony of Irenaeus that the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3; Eusebius, Church History 3.18.2-3). Early-date writers reply that Irenaeus' words may mean that John, not the vision, was seen then.

objections.q: The gospel was not preached to the whole world before AD 70.
objections.a: The Greek word in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene, the inhabited world of the Roman Empire. Luke uses the same word for Augustus' census of "all the world" (Luke 2:1) and for the famine under Claudius (Acts 11:28). Paul writes that the gospel had already been heard in all the world and preached to every creature under heaven (Romans 1:8; Colossians 1:6, 1:23). So this reading holds that the condition was met before the end came in AD 70.

objections.q: Jesus did not visibly return in AD 70.
objections.a: This reading answers that "coming on the clouds" is the Old Testament language of God coming in judgment, as against Egypt, where no one saw a body in the sky. Jesus told the high priest that he would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds, which this reading takes as seeing His judgment in history. Partial preterists add that Matthew 24 describes a coming in judgment in AD 70, but they still expect a future, bodily Second Coming. Full preterists hold that the one promised coming took place in AD 70.

objections.q: The tribulation of AD 70 was not the worst in history.
objections.a: This reading never makes light of later horrors such as the Holocaust. It notes that "never before or after" is a set phrase that Scripture uses for several different events (Exodus 11:6; Ezekiel 5:9; Daniel 9:12; Joel 2:2), so it measures weight rather than counting deaths. AD 70 was unique in covenant meaning: the end of the temple, the priesthood and the sacrifices. Josephus himself wrote that the misfortunes of all nations since the world began were small compared with those of the Jews in that war (Josephus, Jewish War, Preface 4).

objections.q: Luke 21:24 says Jerusalem will be trampled until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. Does that not point to a long age after AD 70?
objections.a: Fulfilled readers answer in two ways. Some link the "times of the Gentiles" to the forty-two months in which the nations trample the holy city (Revelation 11:2), so the phrase describes the war itself. Others accept that Gentile rule over Jerusalem lasted long after AD 70, but note that Luke 21:24 describes what follows the fall of the city. Jesus' time limit (Luke 21:32) covers the things the disciples asked about, which centred on the temple's destruction. Partial preterists often take this second view.

objections.q: Acts 1:11 says Jesus will come back in the same way the disciples saw Him go.
objections.a: Here preterists differ. Partial preterists agree that Acts 1:11 promises a future, bodily, visible return, distinct from the coming in judgment in AD 70. Full preterists answer that "in like manner" points to the manner, not to who would see it: He left in a cloud, seen only by His disciples, and He would come in the cloud of God's glory and judgment. Most churches through history have read Acts 1:11 as a future bodily return.

objections.q: If AD 70 fulfilled Matthew 24, why did the early church not say so?
objections.a: Some early writers did connect much of the discourse with AD 70. Eusebius quoted Jesus' warnings (Matthew 24:19-21) and set them beside Josephus' account of the siege, saying the prophecy was fulfilled (Eusebius, Church History 3.7.1-2). Others, such as John Chrysostom, read the great tribulation in the same way. Yet the same writers also expected a future return of Christ, a bodily resurrection and a final judgment, as the creeds confess. Partial preterists see this as support for their view, while full preterists hold that the fathers did not fully see the time texts.

objections.q: What about the resurrection of the dead in 1 Corinthians 15?
objections.a: This is the main point where fulfilled readers divide. Full preterists tie the resurrection of Daniel 12:2 to the time when the power of the holy people is shattered (Daniel 12:7), and they read it as a corporate, covenant resurrection completed in AD 70. Partial preterists, with nearly all churches through history, hold that the bodily resurrection and the final judgment are still future. They note that Paul warned against those who said the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:17-18). This study presents the full-preterist answer as one view, not the view of the church as a whole.

objections.q: "This generation" means the Jewish race, or the generation that sees the signs, not Jesus' hearers.
objections.a: This reading notes that the Greek word genea means people living at the same time, while a different word, genos, means a race or kind. Every other use of "this generation" in Matthew refers to Jesus' own hearers (Matthew 11:16; 12:41-45; 23:36). In Matthew 23:36 Jesus says that all the judgment He has just described will come on "this generation", only verses before the discourse begins. Jesus also said that some standing there would not die before seeing Him come in His kingdom (Matthew 16:28).

objections.q: Revelation was written around AD 95, so its visions cannot be about AD 70.
objections.a: The fulfilled reading of Matthew 24 does not depend on the date of Revelation, because Jesus spoke around AD 30 and set the limit of "this generation". On Revelation itself, many fulfilled readers argue for a date in the 60s from evidence inside the book, such as the measured temple and the sixth king (see the Revelation dating section). They also note that the key line in Irenaeus can be read in more than one way (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3). Many scholars still hold the later date.

objections.q: Could AD 70 be a first, partial fulfilment, with a greater one still to come?
objections.a: This reading answers that Jesus gave one time limit for "all these things" (Matthew 24:34). He also said the great tribulation would be unlike anything before it or after it (Matthew 24:21), which would rule out a greater repeat. Daniel was told to seal his book because its time was far away, but John was told not to seal his because the time was near (Daniel 12:4; Revelation 22:10). Some partial preterists do see AD 70 as a pattern or preview of the final coming, while full preterists reject any second fulfilment.

mandate.text: If the end of the age came in the first century, what now? The fulfilled reading answers by going back to the beginning. In Genesis 1:28 God blessed the first humans and gave them five commands. Sin distorted that calling, but Christ, the last Adam, restores it. Through one man's sin came condemnation, and through one man's righteousness comes life (Romans 5:18). As He is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17). So believers are not waiting for the world to collapse. They are called to live out the original mandate under the reign of Christ, without fear of the future. Many Christians of other views also teach the creation mandate and faithful stewardship; the fulfilled reading gives it special weight because it holds that the great judgment Jesus foretold is past.

items.label: Be fruitful
items.text: Bear fruit in character and in work. Jesus said His Father is glorified when His disciples bear much fruit (John 15:8). Fruitfulness starts with a life joined to Christ.

items.label: Multiply
items.text: In Acts the word of God spread and the number of disciples multiplied. Share the faith, raise children in it, and train others who will train others (2 Timothy 2:2).

items.label: Fill (replenish)
items.text: The earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory as the waters cover the sea. Bring the life of Christ into every place: home, work, study, art and public life.

items.label: Subdue
items.text: Subduing begins within. Bring every thought under Christ, overcome evil with good (Romans 12:21), and patiently bring order and healing where there is disorder.

items.label: Have dominion
items.text: Those who receive God's grace 'reign in life' through Jesus Christ. Dominion means caring service under the King, not control over others. Christ, who has all authority, sends His people to make disciples of the nations (Matthew 28:18-20).

quiz.q: Which Roman general led the siege that destroyed the temple in AD 70?
quiz.explain: Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, commanded the siege of Jerusalem in AD 70. Pompey took the city in 63 BC, and Hadrian crushed a later revolt in AD 132-135.

quiz.q: Which ancient historian was an eyewitness of the siege of Jerusalem?
quiz.explain: Josephus was with Titus during the siege as an interpreter. Tacitus and Suetonius wrote later from Rome, and Eusebius wrote more than two centuries afterwards.
Josephus dates the burning to the tenth day of the month Lous (Av), in late summer AD 70 (Jewish War 6.4.5). The revolt began in 66 and Masada fell in 73 or 74.

quiz.q: In Matthew 23:36, who are 'this generation' on whom 'all these things' will come?
options: The Jewish people in every age
The people living in Jesus' own day
A generation alive at the end of history
quiz.explain: Jesus was speaking to the scribes and Pharisees in the temple. The fulfilled reading, and many other readers, take 'this generation' here as His own contemporaries.

quiz.q: Which four disciples asked Jesus about these things privately, according to Mark 13:3?
quiz.explain: Mark names Peter, James, John and Andrew, two pairs of brothers. The fulfilled reading stresses that 'you' in the discourse first means them.

quiz.q: Which Roman governor of Syria marched on Jerusalem in AD 66 and then suddenly withdrew?
quiz.explain: Cestius Gallus attacked Jerusalem in the autumn of AD 66, then withdrew and was defeated at Beth-horon (Jewish War 2.19). Many interpreters think this gave Christians a window to flee.

quiz.q: According to Eusebius (Church History 3.5.3), where did the Jerusalem church go before the war?
quiz.explain: Eusebius says the church was warned by a revelation to leave the city and settle in Pella, a town east of the Jordan. The fulfilled reading sees this as obedience to Matthew 24:16.

quiz.q: The Greek word for 'world' in Matthew 24:14 is oikoumene. What does it usually mean?
options: The inhabited world, often the Roman world
quiz.explain: Oikoumene means the inhabited earth. Luke 2:1 uses it for the Roman Empire. Paul could say the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Colossians 1:23) and in all the world (Colossians 1:6).

quiz.q: Which Roman historian wrote that many Jews believed ancient writings foretold men from Judea would rule the world (Histories 5.13)?
quiz.explain: Tacitus records this belief in Histories 5.13. Suetonius reports a similar oracle in Vespasian 4.5. Both say the Romans applied it to Vespasian.

quiz.q: According to Josephus (Jewish War 6.9.3), how many people were taken captive during the whole war?
quiz.explain: Josephus gives 97,000 captives and 1,100,000 dead. Scholars debate his numbers, but these are the figures he reports.

quiz.q: Why was John told not to seal his prophecy (Revelation 22:10)?
options: Because Daniel had already explained it
Because it was only for Gentiles
quiz.explain: John was told not to seal it because the time was at hand. Daniel was told to seal his vision because it referred to days far in the future (Daniel 8:26; 12:4).

quiz.q: Which monument in Rome shows soldiers carrying the temple lampstand in triumph?
quiz.explain: The Arch of Titus was built after Titus' death in AD 81. One relief shows the menorah and other temple objects carried in the victory parade.

quiz.q: What do partial preterists such as R. C. Sproul and Kenneth Gentry still expect in the future?
options: The bodily return of Christ and the resurrection of the dead
quiz.explain: Partial preterists accept that much of Matthew 24 was fulfilled in AD 70, but with the historic creeds they expect a future bodily return, resurrection and final judgment.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five commands of Genesis 1:28?
quiz.explain: The five are: be fruitful, multiply, fill (replenish) the earth, subdue it, and have dominion. The fulfilled reading calls believers to live these out under Christ's reign.
